text.text: Delaying the start of tasks with deadlines is a widespread phenomenon that occurs across multiple domains.
While delaying tasks can be maladaptive, here we propose that, in some situations, it results from an optimal time-management strategy.

We propose a theoretical model of the strategic delay of the initiation of tasks with deadlines that relies on an unavoidable aspect of any projection into the future, namely, that the time it takes to complete a task is variable.

This fundamental assumption distinguishes our theory from alternative theoretical accounts that invoke specific structures of preferences or costs to elucidate the occurrence of (adaptive or maladaptive) task-initiation delays.

Our model captures the basic features of strategic delay and predicts a phenomenon that we demonstrate empirically, the 'farther-earlier' effect: decision-makers who live farther to their destinations (e.g., schools or offices) tend to arrive earlier than those who live closer.
The same theory explains the widely documented tendency to repeatedly delay the initiation of a task (e.g., drafting a grant application) as the deadline for the completion of the task approaches.
Our framework thus puts forth a normative theory in which various manifestations of strategic delay reflect an optimal adaptation to environmental statistics.

Delaying the start of a task bound by a deadline is a pervasive behavioural phenomenon that occurs in diverse forms and in multiple domains: when leaving home to reach the office or the airport, booking a flight, or drafting a grant.
In all these scenarios, people often delay the initiation of the task until the 'last moment'.

Moreover, as deadlines approach, people often reevaluate their choices and end up postponing the initiation of tasks, and thereby often end up completing their tasks prohibitively close to the deadlines (Steel, 2007; Steel et al., 2018).

text.text: Delaying task initiation appears as puzzling because it usually grants only a small benefit but might entail a great cost (Ellis & Knaus, 1977; Harriott & Ferrari, 1996; Silver, 1974; Steel, 2007).

text.text: For this reason, the tendency to delay task initiation has often been associated with procrastination and in turn to maladaptive psychological mechanisms such as avoidance behaviour, self-regulation failure, and motivational deficits.

For example, chronic procrastination is typically characterized as a persistent tendency to delay intended actions despite anticipated negative consequences, and is often associated with subjective anxiety and poor self-efficacy (Sirois, 2004; Solomon & Rothblum, 1984; Steel, 2007).

text.text: However, not all instances of task-initiation delays reflect maladaptive procrastination.

Previous work in economics and psychology has long recognized that delays in carrying out tasks can sometimes be rational-work that appears under the rubrics of "(optimal) time management and planning" and "active" or "strategic delay."
Here, delays are viewed as resulting from adaptive strategies that account for a rational cost-benefit trade-off in time management (Chun Chu & Choi, 2005; Corkin et al., 2011; Klingsieck, 2013).

text.text: In all these approaches, the rationality of delaying task initiation under a deadline follows from assumptions about structure of preference or costs affecting the DMs, or the time dependence of their cognitive state.

These theories largely disregard an important aspect of task statistics that the DM must contend with: namely, that the time required to complete a task is often variable and uncertain, and that this uncertainty can change over time.
This simple and general observation is key to understanding various aspects of task delay in a normative framework, in which the DM's decision process is well-adapted to the task statistics.
Here, we propose a rational model of the delay of the initiation of tasks with deadlines.

The model does not rely on restrictive assumptions on the form of preference or cost; rather, it predicts delay of task initiation as optimal behaviour in the presence of variability in the duration of tasks.
It makes use of a simple idea anticipated by the writer Jean de La Fontaine.

In his 1668 fable, Le Lièvre et la Tortue (The Hare and the Tortoise), the author describes how a slow but regular tortoise reaches a goal before a hare-fast but suffering from distractions and disruptions along its path.
This fable highlights that temporal disruptions can cause even a fast animal to arrive too late.
The question a DM should therefore address is how to avoid being late under temporal uncertainty.
The model of strategic delay proposed here is based on two simple ingredients.
First, under temporal uncertainty, one ought to opt for a safety margin in planning to reach a goal.
Second, the longer the way, the greater the uncertainty.

Based on these two ingredients, a normative prescription to minimize costs under uncertainty predicts strategic delay as an optimal adaptation to temporal uncertainty and captures two key behavioural observations.

First, we show that our normative theory makes a counterintuitive prediction, which we call 'farther-earlier' effect: DMs who live farther from a target location (e.g., school or office) should arrive earlier (or delay their trip to a lesser degree) than those who live closer.

Alternative theories based on the rational trade-off of the two costs of leaving too early and arriving after the deadline would predict the opposite pattern: that DMs who live farther would incur more delay as a way to save on the cost of leaving exceedingly early.
By providing empirical evidence for the 'farther-earlier' effect in a controlled experimental study, we validate the model's prediction.

Second, we show that the theory addresses the recursive nature of delaying task initiation: the observation that, as the deadline approaches, DMs often re-evaluate a decision to initiate a task and tend to postpone initiation repeatedly (Steel, 2007; Steel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Second, we show that the theory addresses the recursive nature of delaying task initiation: the observation that, as the deadline approaches, DMs often re-evaluate a decision to initiate a task and tend to postpone initiation repeatedly <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Steel, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Steel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This phenomenon, often associated with maladaptive procrastination, emerges in our account as a simple consequence of the fact that, as the deadline approaches, the intrinsic variability of task completion time diminishes.
Thus, according to our approach, these puzzles do not constitute 'irrational biases' but rather can reflect optimal behaviour in the presence of uncertainty in the duration of tasks.
In sum, our proposed explanation frames the phenomenon of delaying the initiation of tasks with deadlines as optimal time management in the face of the randomness inherent in human actions.
It also unifies disparate observations, some of which cannot be explained simply as a rational trade-off in a deterministic setting on the basis of specific structure of costs.

In deciding when to initiate a task (e.g., drive to the office), there is a trade-off between the cost of starting too early (e.g., spending less time with one's family at home) and the cost of completing the task too late (e.g., overshooting the deadline).
In a deterministic environment, one would set the starting time so as to end the task precisely at the deadline.
In reality, however, the duration of any task is variable or uncertain, either because of extraneous factors (e.g., traffic) or internal ones (e.g., tiredness).
As a result, the trade-off is statistical: optimal behaviour results from minimizing the total expected cost.
In order to construct a quantitative model, we must specify the nature of the variability.
While the predicted trends will not depend on its detailed form, for the sake of simplicity we will assume that the variability in the duration of a task obeys a normal distribution.

For the same reason, it is beneficial to account for a 'safety margin,' namely, to include a 'buffer' time window separating the expected termination time, 𝑡 *0. , and the deadline, 𝑡 .

Our theory of strategic delay predicts a phenomenon we call 'farther-earlier' effect: the fact that DMs located farther from a target (e.g., a school or an office) to be reached by a deadline tend to arrive earlier (or with less delay) than those who are located closer.

According to our model, this behaviour is optimal because a longer task (larger 𝑇 "#$% ) comes with a larger variance in task duration (𝜎 "#$% C ) as a consequence, a larger 'safety margin' is required.

We illustrate this mechanism with a simple example in which two DMs, Jane and Charles, who live 14 and 7 minutes (on average) away from an office complex, respectively, must start work by 8AM to avoid being sanctioned.

In the morning, both Jane and Charles would like to leave their home as late as possible (according to the early cost, i.e., the cost of initiating too early, purple curve in Fig. 1A), but fear arriving at work later than 8AM (according to the late cost, i.e., the cost of terminating too late, orange curve in Fig. 1A).

text.text: This result holds under two mild assumptions in our model; namely, that the late cost increases monotonically with lag from the deadline (here, we carry out calculations with costs that scale with a power of the lag) and that the standard deviation of task duration grows with its mean value (again, we carry out calculations with a power-law dependence of the standard deviation on the mean).

In sum, if Jane and Charles adopt strategic delay -namely, they are aware of the uncertainty on commute durations and they leave their houses as late as possible, given the risk of arriving at work after the deadline -Jane will arrive sooner at work than Charles on average.
This 'fartherearlier' effect results from a rational estimation of the expected cost in a stochastic context.
To our knowledge, the 'farther-earlier' effect predicted by our model has never been assessed in a controlled experimental setting.
To examine it, we designed an online experiment that mimics the example of Jane and Charles described above.
In the experimental task, participants (n=45) had to navigate in a 2D virtual environment composed of a "treasure room" and a "hallway" (Fig. 2).

In the simple model described above, we considered a single process -the initiation of a task -and we showed that the initiation time is a function of both the mean and the variance of the task's duration.
The model did not, however, account for how and when the initiation time was set in the first place.

In an extended model, we instead consider two coupled processes: first, the DM sets an initiation time, well before the task is actually initiated (e.g., deciding early in the morning when to leave the house); second, later on the DM initiates the task (e.g., actually leaving home).

Our approach indicates that the widely reported tendency for people to further delay task initiation precisely when they had planned to start the task -and hence to complete a task late soon before the deadline (Steel, 2007) -does not necessarily reflect maladaptive procrastination, but can instead result from optimal adaptation to uncertainty in the durations of both task and planning.

Observations of delays in initiating tasks with deadlines are common but puzzling.
Why do people who live closer to their destination tend to arrive later than those who live farther?
Why do people repeatedly postpose the start of intended tasks when a deadline approaches?

While many instances of delaying tasks are associated with maladaptive procrastination and psychological processes such as poor self-control and anxiety (Sirois, 2004; Solomon & Rothblum, 1984; Steel, 2007), not all cases need reflect dysfunction.

text.text: Here, we develop a framework in which delaying the initiation of tasks with deadlines emerges as an optimal strategy for managing time subject to uncertainty in the duration of tasks.
Our account connects to previous work in economics and psychology that examined action delays in terms of (optimal) time management and planning.
In this context, authors have alluded to 'active' or 'strategic delay' (Chun Chu & Choi, 2005; Corkin et al., 2011; Klingsieck, 2013).

text.text: In these accounts, strategic delay is conceptualized in terms of a trade-off between the cost of early task initiation and the cost of completing the task too late (Ellenberg, 2015).

text.text: Unlike these theoretical approaches (discussed below), our proposal does not assume particular or time-dependent forms of preference or cost but instead takes as its central assumption the uncertainty in task duration.
Specifically, our approach assumes that people take real-world temporal statistics into account when planning.
Our approach also assumes that temporal uncertainty grows with mean duration.
This assumption is natural since a longer duration presents more opportunities for disruption.

It is also in agreement with empirical observation: various studies in different cities and countries (Australia, Chile, China) have reported a linear relation between the mean travel time and the standard deviation of travel time, in the contexts of walking as well as traveling by car, bus, and subway (Durán-Hormazábal & Tirachini, 2016).

text.text: Based on this statistical assumption, our model captures key features of strategic delay.

One such feature is the 'farther-earlier' effect: people who live farther from a destination tend to arrive earlier (or procrastinate less) than those who live closer, a trend which is not explained naturally based on forms of preference.
We reproduced this trend in a laboratory experiment in which we manipulated the statistics of temporal uncertainty.
While -to the best of our knowledge -ours is the first laboratory demonstration of the 'farther-earlier' effect, this effect has also been reported in real-life situations.

For example, a 2015 study of transportation dynamics funded by the cities of Lafayette, Orinda, and Moraga found that "People that live closest to the BART stations (in Lafayette and Orinda) are more likely to report not being able to find parking within the BART lots in the last 30 days than are people who live farther away (in Moraga or outside Lamorinda), suggesting that residents living farther away plan ahead and arrive earlier at BART, knowing the parking constraints" (Lamorinda Program Management Committee, 2015).

A two stage extension of our model also explains the tendency of people to repeatedly postpone the initiation of a task, as the deadline approaches -a feature often associated with maladaptive procrastination, because each delay invalidates an earlier decision (Steel, 2007; Steel et al., 2018).

text.text: This extension assumes that the task-initiation time is chosen under uncertainty on both task duration and the time of task initiation itself.
Because the latter ban be estimated more precisely as it approaches, the optimal initiation time is postponed, as a revision of an earlier decision.
The two-stage model extension does not imply a new form of optimality; it illustrates dynamics in which DMs repeatedly revise earlier decisions as planning uncertainty decreases.
The additional prediction of the two-stage model is therefore a form of recursive delay through successive-re-evaluations, even when preferences and cost functions remain unchanged.
Here, strategic and repeated delays do not result from exotic forms of preference nor from a maladaptive process, but from optimal adaptation to an uncertain environment.

text.text: Most of these theories do not provide a rationale for the 'farther-earlier' effect.

In formulations involving temporally discounted cost, the prediction would in fact be reversed: individuals residing farther from the destination would value delaying departure more than those residing closer.

Symmetrically, in urgency-based formulations, one could argue that individuals living closer to the destination would feel more compelled to depart than those who perceive the deadline as temporally more distant.

Models incorporating task aversiveness and its increasing salience as the task approaches could, however, offer a justification for the effect, as individuals who live farther depart earlier because they perceive less aversiveness toward the task.
In contrast to these proposals, our model does not assume specific forms of time-dependent cost, aversiveness, or sense of urgency, but instead makes use of a statistical argument.
It is interesting, however, to examine whether the two types of approaches might be more closely related than they appear.
While temporal discounting can give rise to a rich phenomenology and can explain various puzzles, its own foundation remains to be fully elucidated.
It has been proposed that temporal discounting can be viewed normatively when a DM takes future uncertainty into account (Gabaix & Laibson, 2017).
text.formatted: It has been proposed that temporal discounting can be viewed normatively when a DM takes future uncertainty into account <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gabaix & Laibson, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while a phenomenology of preference modulation might explain puzzling behavioural trends, underlying it might be a correct apprehension of fixed preferences and costs together with environmental statistics by the DM.

It is also worth noting that, in contrast to theories emphasizing the role of motivation and emotion on task-initiation delaying and procrastination, our approach views delay as a rational strategy to achieve goals while minimising costs-motivation does not enter the picture.

Yet another account of procrastination, based on ideas from reinforcement learning, has been proposed to explain why a rational agent would delay the initiation of a task at the expense of a subsequent greater expenditure of effort (P. Zhang & Ma, 2019).

text.text: As in our work, this approach views procrastination as an adaptive process: the DM adapts to the rate of reward provided by the environment, whereas in our model the DM adapts to temporal uncertainty.
Finally, our model is closely related to probabilistic (Bayesian) approaches to perception and action in cognitive and motor neuroscience (Doya et al., 2007; Parr et al., 2022; Pouget et al., 2013).

text.text: Our experimental and theoretical results can be viewed as a temporal counterpart of the near-optimal accounting of uncertainty in decisionmaking.

While it is gratifying that a simple framework such as the one reported on in this paper can explain various empirical observations on task-initiation delaying as optimal adaptation to environmental statistics, obviously such a simple approach is bound to yield only a very partial picture of a rich phenomenology.
Furthermore, we do not suggest that all forms of delays under deadlines can be viewed as rational adaptation: DMs may also exhibit sub-optimal procrastination.
Various studies have shown that DMs occasionally procrastinate in daily situations, even in situations in which delays lead to harmful consequences.

This maladaptive procrastination may arise from individual cognitive, motivational, and personality factors, including poor self-control or anxiety (Sirois, 2004; Solomon & Rothblum, 1984; Steel, 2007), poor perception of the passage of time (Conte & Jacobs, 2003), and excessive reliance on multitasking (DeLonzor, 2013) -mechanisms that fall outside the scope of our model, but that can co-exist with rational adaptation to uncertainty.

text.text: Here, we have not attempted to advance a unified theory of every type of delay under deadlines but instead asked which ones can be understood as strategic or optimal adaptations to environmental (temporal) statistics.
The model can be extended in various ways.
More involved forms of rewards and costs can be included.
The numerical parameters entering the model can themselves become functions of psychological variables, such as personality traits.

More concretely, the current model considers only the costs associated with starting a task too early and ending it too late, but not other costs such as the effort required to execute the task itself.
If an added task cost depends only on the nature of the task and not on its duration, our conclusions remain unchanged.
If, however, the task cost depends on the task duration, it can affect the model predictions.

Crucially, the effect will depend on whether the task cost increases or decreases with task duration -one can easily imagine examples of both types -and the two cases will lead to different conclusions.
In the latter case, we expect qualitatively similar conclusions and a stronger effect.

In the former case, an extended model would involve a trade-off between delaying task initiation and compensating subsequently through increased effort, in line with the observation that individuals sometimes complete tasks under time pressure by investing more effort than necessary to meet deadlines (Steel et al., 2018).

text.text: A feature of our model is that it focuses on situations in which explicit deadlines are present.

However, people also incur delays in situations that do not necessarily involve external deadlines, such as answering e-mails, cleaning the house, donating blood, going to the gym, or scheduling a medical check-up.

While at least some of these scenarios are plausibly related to maladaptive forms of procrastination -and influenced by motivational and psychological processes (e.g., anxiety or lack of self-control) beyond the scope of the current model -future extensions of the model may be able to account for at least some of the phenomenology.

Indeed, although our equations and simulations assumed explicit deadlines, the model itself does not require the cost function to increase abruptly at a deadline; it is sufficient that the expected cost increases over time, as is the case for some of the examples mentioned above.

More generally, the model can be extended to time-sensitive tasks, that is, tasks for which postponement entails an increased cost, regardless of whether this increase is induced by an explicit deadline or through a smooth temporal mechanism.
It is also possible that even in the absence of explicit deadlines, DMs often impose internal deadlines on themselves as a way of self-regulation (Ariely & Wertenbroch, 2002).

text.text: Incorporating self-imposed deadlines would naturally extend the current framework to tasks lacking externally imposed deadlines; in that case, the issue would shift to explaining, on a normative basis, the necessity of internal deadlines.

text.text: In the experimental task, participants had to navigate in a 2D virtual environment composed of a "treasure room" and a "hallway".
The goal of a participant was to collect as many coins as possible in the treasure room and then reach the exit at the end of the hallway before a deadline indicated by a visible countdown.
Each trial had a maximum duration of 30 seconds, during which coins spawned in random positions in the treasure room, at a constant rate.
The maximum number of coins that could spawn was 60.
If participants failed to reach the exit before the deadline, they received a penalty of 100 coins, and lost the coins collected in that trial.
Participants began with a total of 100 coins.

To reach the exit, participants had to leave the room through a door that would close behind their avatar to prevent them from backtracking, and then to cross a hallway interrupted by a number of doors.
To open a door, participants had to bring their avatar in contact with it, and the door would then gradually open over some duration.
Once participants reached the exit, they had to wait for the end of the countdown, as a way to prevent them from quitting the experiment any sooner.

During this time, they were shown relevant information, such as the number of coins they collected during the trial, the total amount of coins they possessed at that instant, the time at which they left the room, and the time remaining before the deadline.
The main variable of interest we examined in this work is the estimated arrival time (EAT) of the participant avatar to the exit platform.
The EAT calculation is based upon the time at which the avatar left the "treasure room" summed with the average time needed to move across the hallway for that trial condition.

The behavioural experiment was divided in two blocks of 24 trials each, one for each experimental condition -Long hallway or Short hallway (see Fig. 2)-mimicking the case of a DM living farther or closer to a target destination, respectively.

text.text: The order of blocks was randomized across participants.
The first four trials in each block were practice trials; they had no effect on the final score and were excluded from the analyses.
The Long-and Short-hallway conditions comprised 1 and 4 doors respectively.
The time each door needed to open was variable, with a mean of 1.5 seconds and a standard deviation that depended on the number of doors (σ1 Door=0.15s, σ4 Doors =0.6s).
This design ensured that the standard deviation of the commuting time through the hallway was proportional to its mean, thus adhering to the assumptions in the model.
We recruited 50 participants between the ages of 18 and 40 years old through the online platform Prolific.
Participant gave informed consent online prior to participation and we remunerated them according to their game score.
After pre-processing stage (see below for exclusion criteria), we included 45 individuals in the analysis.
Of the participants, 26 identified as male, 16 as female, 2 as other, and 1 preferred not to say.
The mean age was 29, with a standard deviation of 6, and all participants were located in the United States and the United Kingdom.
All the procedures were approved by the CNR Ethics committee.
